doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: How he came to reissue projects
summary: Why he takes on reissues, his 78 transfers at WKCR, and how the CD age brought producer work.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yeah. What attracts you — I’m skipping ahead years, but what attracts you to take on a reissue project?

Well the importance of the music. The ability to make it a superior presentation to contemporary and potentially future audiences from the way it was initially presented, to document the information you know that might otherwise not be preserved. Those are three real reasons.
And is it something that you usually initiate or is it a record company coming to you?

Well originally I offered my services as a provider of the rarer stuff with the ability to convert it into a suitable sound for their reissues or first time issues. You know like I had actually a completely different system of doing 78 transfers in the mid-seventies, which I wonder if I ever again will be able to do and then find out if there was anything to it. But I used to do my re-mastering — KCR at that time was still off the air. This is how long ago it was because I’m sure it’s over 25 years ago, was off the air for a couple of hours in the middle of the night in those years. It wasn’t yet 24 hours a day. And I would do my re-mastering then on the premises and would throw it up to the exciter. There’s a thing that triggers the transmitter having enough power to — it’s sort of like a preamp for radio. And I would throw it through the exciter and then download, to use a modern term that was not used at the time, and transfer, tap off. I would bring it across from the exciter to a fairly good Scully two track machine, which was two track mono of course. I wish I had, if I was really smart I would have done a four track mono because they were mono. And that was my system then. And I’ve had so a little — so they said well you really know about the music, you write the notes. So I did a couple of liner notes, I did a couple of transfers, and then eventually I did a couple where I did both on the same project. And I would say that it was a very small component of my career. It was not happening that often, for another reason why it was so small, it was literally small as well as it was a small ad. Because I was doing the radio, I was trying to teach or trying to — I was still running the West End which we haven’t talked about, a night club that had jazz seven nights a week for 17 years with very heavy hitting people like Jo Jones and others and Dizzy Gillespie and Benny Carter and others. And then I think the CD age is responsible for that. Because suddenly there was going to be more re-issuing. And by this time my reputation, I was a little bit older, I must have been in my early thirties now and so there’s a guy who’s got the rare stuff we don’t have who can do the audio work, who can write
and also has producer capabilities. Well that’s one stop shopping. Let’s do him. And I think that’s how it happened.
